phases.label: The road to war
phases.description: After the break between the two leaders, Octavian has war declared on Cleopatra and Antony is stripped of his consulship, while Antony gathers his forces and Cleopatra's fleet and treasure at Ephesus, then at Samos and Athens, and winters at Patrae; the following spring both armies and fleets cross to western Greece and take up positions around Actium, with challenges, offers of battle and defections already passing between the camps.

phases.label: Antony's position isolated
phases.description: Agrippa's fleet seizes Methone, Leucas, Patrae and Corinth and raids the Greek coasts, while Octavian fortifies a camp on the height north of the gulf and blockades Antony by land and sea, cutting his supplies and communications and shutting his fleet in the Ambracian Gulf in a deadlock.

phases.label: Attrition and desertion
phases.description: Antony's camp is worn down by sickness, hunger and failed skirmishes and cavalry actions, while Domitius, Dellius, Amyntas, Plancus and allied kings desert to Octavian, some carrying word of Antony's plans, and Antony and Cleopatra quarrel over strategy and her presence.

phases.label: The council and the decision
phases.description: In Antony's camp, generals and Roman officers argue over fighting on land, retreating inland, or fighting at sea, with some urging that Cleopatra be sent home, until Cleopatra's advice for breaking the blockade by sea prevails; Antony then burns surplus ships, mans the best ones, carries sails aboard and secretly loads treasure for a breakout.

phases.label: The fleets deploy
phases.description: After storms delay the plan, Antony embarks troops on his tall, timber-protected ships and forms his fleet in lines outside the straits, while Octavian and Agrippa address and embark their forces, form three divisions and wait out at sea, and the two fleets hold off and hesitate before coming to an engagement as the land armies watch from shore.

phases.label: The lines engage
phases.description: The fleets meet outside the gulf and fight a long, indecisive battle in which Octavian's lighter ships dash in, swarm, and shatter oars while Antony's tall ships shoot from towers and grapple, with neither side ramming much, as wings are extended to outflank and the lines are strung out, while Cleopatra's squadron waits at anchor behind the fighting.

phases.label: Cleopatra's squadron breaks through
phases.description: Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships hoists sail, passes through or behind the fighting with the treasure aboard, and makes for the open sea and Egypt before a rising wind, with Agrippa's ships letting it go or taking only a couple of stragglers.

phases.label: Antony follows Cleopatra
phases.description: Antony abandons the fight and his men, boards a fast galley and is taken aboard Cleopatra's flagship, where he sits silent and brooding at the prow, fends off a few pursuing ships, and sails with her via Tænarus and the Peloponnesus toward Africa and Egypt, where Cleopatra enters Alexandria feigning victory.

phases.label: The remaining fleet is defeated
phases.description: With Cleopatra and Antony gone, the rest of the fleet keeps fighting, beating off boarders until Octavian's men use fire, which spreads through the ships and kills men by flame, sea and each other's hands, until the survivors surrender or are burned or sunk and a large part of the fleet is captured.

phases.label: The army surrenders
phases.description: Antony's land army, left under Canidius, waits several days and then loses its commanders, who flee, and the troops go over to Octavian and the vassal kings lay down arms; Octavian occupies the camp, offers lenient terms, spares some such as Sosius, and goes to Athens as Greece submits, though one account has him massacring Antony's adherents.

phases.label: Meaning and memory
phases.description: Octavian commemorates the victory by founding Nicopolis on the site of his camp, building a larger temple and shrine of Apollo, dedicating captured ships, and establishing the Actian games every September, along with monuments such as the Campsite Memorial.
